lexical.adversarial_notes: I searched for the origin and history of the 'Roman thumbs up/down = gladiator live/die' narrative framing using multiple queries targeting: (1) the general history and myth-busting of the framing; (2) pre-2003 sources including books, encyclopedias, and films; (3) the 1872 Gérôme painting 'Pollice Verso' as a known historical anchor; (4) early film representations including Ben-Hur (1959), Spartacus (1960), and Gladiator (2000); and (5) scholarly and translation sources from the 17th century onward. The proposed 2003-01-01 date is decisively refuted: the narrative framing is demonstrably centuries old. The canonical modern version (thumbs up = live, thumbs down = die) was firmly established by Gérôme's 1872 painting, which was exhibited in New York City and sparked a 26-page scholarly pamphlet rebuttal by 1879. A proto-version of the framing (thumb gesture = gladiator fate) appears in John Dryden's 1693 English translation of Juvenal's Satires and a 1601 English translation of Pliny. The 2000 film 'Gladiator' is the most prominent modern amplifier, predating 2003 by three years. Near-misses considered and ruled out: I considered whether the proposed 2003 date might refer to a specific academic paper or debunking article rather than the framing itself — but the framing (not the debunking) is what was proposed as originating in 2003, and the evidence overwhelmingly refutes that. Limitations: Google Books archives, Usenet/forum archives, and paywalled newspaper archives from the 19th and early 20th centuries were not directly accessible in this search, but the secondary sources consulted are consistent and mutually corroborating across many independent outlets.

sources.title: Juvenal, Satires (c. 100–127 CE) — 'infesto pollice' passage
sources.description: Roman satirist Juvenal uses the phrase 'infesto pollice' ('hostile thumb') in connection with the crowd signaling death for a gladiator, one of the few surviving primary Latin literary references to a thumb gesture in the arena.
sources.notes: Establishes that thumb gestures were genuinely used in the Roman arena, but the phrase 'hostile thumb' does not specify direction — it is the uncontested anchor for all subsequent debate.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (XXVIII.25) — 'pollices premere'
sources.description: Pliny uses the phrase 'pollices premere,' which can be translated as 'thumb pressed down,' 'thumb squeezed inside the palm,' or 'thumb pressed to the hand,' and describes it as a gesture of acceptance or favor — not condemnation.
sources.notes: A primary Latin source suggesting a concealed or pressed thumb meant approval/mercy, directly contradicting the popular thumbs-up = life reading and suggesting the gesture system was more complex.

sources.title: Aurelius Prudentius, Libri contra Symmachum (c. 402 CE) — 'converso pollice'
sources.description: Christian poet Prudentius describes a Vestal Virgin signaling with her thumb that a victorious gladiator should pierce his fallen opponent's breast, using the phrase 'converso pollice' (turned thumb). His account is one of the most specific ancient descriptions of the death gesture.
sources.notes: A primary source that describes a thumb gesture signaling death but still does not specify direction; later inspired Gérôme's painting and thus the modern myth.

sources.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Pollice Verso (painting, 1872)
sources.description: French academic painter Gérôme depicted Vestal Virgins and Roman spectators giving a thumbs-down gesture to condemn a fallen gladiator. The painting was purchased by a U.S. magnate and exhibited in New York, then later directly inspired Ridley Scott's film Gladiator (2000), cementing the thumbs-down = death reading in popular culture.
sources.status_notes: Historical accuracy of the thumbs-down gesture was challenged within months of the painting's public display, and a 26-page pamphlet in 1879 compiled evidence for and against its accuracy.
sources.notes: The single most influential source for the popular claim; widely identified by scholars as the origin of the modern misconception rather than a reliable record of Roman practice.

sources.title: Anthony Corbeill, Nature Embodied: Gesture in Ancient Rome (Princeton University Press, 2004)
sources.description: The most cited modern scholarly monograph on Roman gesture. Corbeill, a classical studies professor, argues based on literary and sculptural evidence that thumbs-up signaled killing a gladiator, while a closed fist with a wraparound thumb meant sparing him — the reverse of the popular claim.
sources.notes: The leading academic authority on the topic; directly inverts the popular claim by arguing thumbs-up meant death and a concealed thumb meant mercy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pollice verso — scholarly consensus summary
sources.description: The Wikipedia article on pollice verso synthesizes the scholarly debate, noting that the precise gesture and its meaning remain contested, and that according to Corbeill, thumbs-up signaled killing while a closed fist meant sparing.
sources.notes: Useful tertiary synthesis but aggregator entry draws on secondary and primary sources; treats Corbeill as the leading authority while noting the debate is unresolved.

sources.title: Phoenix Art Museum blog on Gérôme's Pollice Verso
sources.description: The museum that holds the original Gérôme painting notes that while a modern reading of thumbs-down as a death signal is widespread, 'there are no historical records that confirm this,' and that the reading was likely reinforced by the film Gladiator.
sources.notes: Institutional voice (the painting's custodian) explicitly distancing the artwork from historical accuracy, reinforcing the dispute direction.

sources.title: Tastes of History: 'Dispelling Some Myths: Thumbs Up'
sources.description: A history education site explains that the Latin phrase pollice verso means only 'with a turned thumb' and does not specify direction; it is uncertain from historical, archaeological, and literary records whether the thumb was turned up, down, horizontally, or concealed.
sources.notes: Accessible secondary synthesis of the scholarly consensus; disputes the specific directional claim (thumbs-up = live, thumbs-down = die) while affirming that thumb gestures were used.

sources.title: Imperium Romanum: 'Pollice verso' — Latin source analysis
sources.description: Analyzes the surviving Latin phrases (pollice verso, infesto pollice, converso pollice, pollices premere) and concludes that current research suggests a thumb pressed against the index finger (fist) signified mercy, while a protruding thumb — direction unspecified — meant a deadly blow.
sources.notes: Redirects from the thumbs-up/down binary to a fist-vs-extended-thumb distinction, suggesting the relevant variable was concealment, not direction.

sources.title: Roman Empire Times: 'Thumbs Down to the Myth'
sources.description: Argues that before Gérôme's 1872 painting, scholars supported the idea that thumbs-down signaled mercy ('throw your sword down'), and that Gérôme misread the Latin word verso as 'turned down' rather than simply 'turned,' reversing the gesture's meaning for modern audiences.
sources.notes: Offers the alternative hypothesis that thumbs-down meant mercy (sword down), not death — a distinct redirecting interpretation from the Corbeill thumbs-up-means-death reading; source is opinion-venue with no direct citation of primary scholarship.

sources.title: Spoken Past: 'Thumbs Down: The Gladiator Gesture Rome Never Used'
sources.description: Synthesizes modern scholarly opinion that Romans likely extended thumbs upward or outward to signal death (mimicking a sword thrust), while concealing thumbs in a closed fist meant mercy — and that Gérôme's painting likely reversed the actual Roman practice.
sources.notes: Recent synthesis aligning with Corbeill; disputes both the thumbs-up = live and thumbs-down = death readings, but is an opinion-venue secondary source.

sources.title: 1601 English translation of Pliny / John Dryden's 1693 Juvenal translation
sources.description: A 1601 translation of Pliny equates the thumb gesture with 'assent' or 'favor,' and Dryden's 1693 translation of Juvenal's Satires gives the thumb being 'bent back, not down' as the death signal — early modern interpretations that predate Gérôme and suggest a different gestural reading.
sources.notes: Pre-Gérôme translations suggest early modern scholars did not read the gesture as thumbs-down = death; redirects toward a 'bent back' or 'assent' interpretation, complicating the binary.

sources.title: Gladiatorial combat: role of the editor (munerator) in deciding fate
sources.description: Historical sources confirm that the final decision on a defeated gladiator's fate rested not with the crowd but with the editor — the official hosting and paying for the spectacle — who could override crowd sentiment. The crowd's gesture was advisory, not binding.
sources.notes: Uncontested background fact that complicates the popular image of a crowd-controlled binary verdict; the gesture system was real but its authority was more nuanced than the myth suggests.

sources.title: Gladiatorial games as public spectacle and capital punishment in ancient Rome
sources.description: Gladiators were typically enslaved people, convicted criminals, or prisoners of war. The arena served simultaneously as entertainment and a theater of justice, with executions reinforcing legal authority — providing essential context for why life-or-death gestures carried public meaning.
sources.notes: Uncontested historical background accepted by all sides; establishes why a standardized gestural system for life-or-death decisions would have existed and mattered.

sources.title: Ridley Scott's Gladiator (2000) and the painting's direct influence on modern perception
sources.description: Producers showed Gérôme's Pollice Verso painting to director Ridley Scott before he read the script; Scott described it as speaking to him of 'the Roman Empire in all its glory and wickedness.' The film then cemented the thumbs-up = live, thumbs-down = die reading for a global audience.
sources.notes: Documents the direct transmission chain from Gérôme's historically disputed painting to the film that most powerfully shaped contemporary popular belief in the claim.

evidence_landscape.summary: The popular claim — thumbs-up meant live, thumbs-down meant die in the Roman arena — rests on a transmission chain that runs from ambiguous Latin texts through a disputed 1872 painting (Gérôme's Pollice Verso) to the 2000 film Gladiator, rather than on clear ancient evidence. The uncontested common ground is that thumb gestures were genuinely used in the Roman arena to signal a gladiator's fate, as attested by Juvenal, Pliny, and Prudentius; but none of these primary sources specifies the direction of the thumb. The leading modern scholarly authority, Anthony Corbeill (Princeton, 2004), argues the actual system was the inverse of the popular claim — thumbs-up signaled death, a concealed fist meant mercy — while other scholars suggest the key variable was concealment vs. extension rather than up vs. down. The overall landscape strongly disputes the specific directional binary of the popular claim while affirming that a gestural system existed; the evidence base is thin (a handful of Latin phrases, no surviving iconography from the arena itself), leaving the precise gesture genuinely unresolved.
evidence_landscape.search_notes: Searched for primary Latin sources, the Gérôme painting's reception history, and Corbeill's scholarly monograph. Under-covered: Desmond Morris's zoological/anthropological work on thumb gestures across cultures, and any potential archaeological evidence (mosaics, reliefs) that might depict arena gestures directly — the near-total absence of such iconographic evidence is itself a significant finding noted by multiple sources.
